passage: No, no, I'm fine, Nitin, honestly. Look, I drew it out. This circle is me, secure-ish, maybe a bit avoidant under stress. This one's Tanya: anxious, textbook. When I pulled back during placements, she chased; when she chased, I pulled back more. It's a loop. There's a whole chapter on it in that psychology elective. So the breakup was structural. Nobody's fault. And here, three more pages: I mapped every fight from July to November by trigger. Seventeen fights. Nine were about how fast I replied to texts. It's kind of fascinating as data. Her last message said, "Varun, you're a boyfriend who reads the manual instead of the room." Which, fine, is also a pattern. What? No, I'm not avoiding anything. I'm doing the opposite. I'm analysing it. I don't see the point of lying in my room feeling sad when I can understand it. Pass the chai. Why are you looking at me like that?

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]
passage: Three days after Rekha's boyfriend Dev ended things, our hostel room had a whiteboard in it. I'm Simran, her roommate, so I watched it fill up. Boxes marked "avoidant" and "anxious", arrows labelled "protest behaviour", a timeline from their first coffee to the last phone call. At midnight she explained it to me like a seminar: "His dismissiveness activated my attachment system. It's predictable, actually." The theory sounded right. She's top of our psychology batch. But when I asked, "Do you miss him?" she picked up the marker and added another arrow. She hasn't played her music since Sunday. She eats dinner reading articles about attachment styles. I can't tell what's happening inside her. I only know the whiteboard is getting fuller and she is getting quieter.

qa.q: What appeared in the hostel room three days after the breakup?
qa.a: A whiteboard with boxes, arrows and a timeline.

qa.q: Why might Rekha answer 'Do you miss him?' by adding another arrow?
qa.a: The theory is real and she is good at it, but it lets her stay in her head, which may feel safer than admitting how much she misses Dev.

qa.q: What could Simran try the next time the midnight seminar starts?
qa.a: Simran could put the whiteboard aside, sit with Rekha, and mention that the music has stopped, inviting her to say how it felt rather than why it happened.

qa.q: What is it like for Simran to share the room during these days?
qa.a: Simran is watching a friend grow quieter, unsure whether to respect the analysis or worry about what it is covering.

grounding: A roommate watches a psychology student turn her breakup into diagrams and theory while growing quieter and avoiding the question of whether she misses him.

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Omkar spread a sheet of chart paper across the canteen table. "Look, Tushar. Pia's attachment style is anxious, mine is avoidant. The breakup was basically predictable." He had drawn arrows in three colours. Tushar asked how he was sleeping. Omkar talked about attachment research for twenty minutes.
Thursday. The chart had a new section: "Communication errors, week by week." Tushar noticed that Omkar left his samosa untouched and kept checking his phone, then turning it face down. "Do you feel bad at all?" Tushar asked. "Feelings are just data," Omkar said.
The next Sunday. Tushar found him on the hostel terrace, the chart folded in his lap. "I keep explaining it," Omkar said quietly, "because explaining is easier than saying I really miss her." Tushar sat down beside him, and for a while neither of them said anything.

qa.q: Where did Tushar find Omkar the next Sunday?
qa.a: On the hostel terrace, the chart folded in his lap.

qa.q: What does Omkar checking his phone and turning it face down suggest he was feeling on Thursday?
qa.a: It hints he was still hoping to hear from Pia and was hurting, even while he insisted feelings were just data.

qa.q: Which choice of Tushar's helped make the terrace admission possible?
qa.a: Tushar kept asking about sleep and feelings instead of debating the chart, and on Sunday Tushar simply sat down, which gave Omkar room to say he missed Pia.

qa.q: What might Tushar have felt during twenty minutes of attachment research on Monday?
qa.a: Probably worried or frustrated, since a simple question about sleep got a lecture back instead of an answer about how Omkar was doing.

grounding: Over several days a student analyses his breakup with colour-coded attachment charts, until he admits the explaining has been a way of not feeling how much he misses her.

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]
passage:
"Abhinav, put the pens down a minute. I can see the arrows from here. Let your Yusuf mamu tell you something.
When I was twenty, studying psychology in Aligarh, Shabnam ended things with me in the library, in about four sentences. That night I filled half a register. Her anxious style, my avoidant one, the push-pull, the exact week it tipped. I even drew a graph of how often we'd spoken.
My roommate Kishore asked, 'But how are you?' I gave him a twenty-minute lecture on attachment styles. He listened, then said, 'That's how it works. I asked how you are.'
I was annoyed. But I couldn't answer.
Everything in that register was correct, beta. It was also a very neat wall. Two weeks later I sat on the hostel stairs and cried for an hour, and only then did the diagrams start to help."

qa.q: What did Kishore ask young Yusuf after the breakup?
qa.a: "But how are you?"

qa.q: Why did filling half a register feel better to young Yusuf than answering Kishore?
qa.a: Mapping styles and graphs made the breakup make sense and felt like control, so the hurt of being left in four sentences could stay behind the analysis.

qa.q: What turning point let the diagrams become useful for Yusuf?
qa.a: Crying on the hostel stairs; once the hurt was actually felt, the understanding had something to help with instead of standing in for it.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt after the twenty-minute lecture?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt the question had been dodged, and cared enough to point out gently that the theory answered how it works, not how Yusuf was.

grounding: Shows, in an uncle's memory, a student explaining a breakup through attachment theory and graphs, where the correct analysis also served as a wall against the hurt.

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]
passage:
The Pune–Nagpur night train was packed, the fan in coach S4 had died, and the network kept dropping. Irawati, twenty, held the phone to her ear anyway.
"So, Mitali, I've worked it out. Asif has an avoidant attachment style, I lean anxious. When I asked for more time together, he withdrew, I pushed, and the cycle fed itself. It's textbook." Her notebook lay open on her knees: a diagram, arrows in two colours.
"Okay," Mitali said, crackly. "But how are you?"
"I just told you. It makes total sense."
The call dropped. She redialled: no signal. With no one left to explain it to, Irawati sat in the stuffy dark while the train rocked. Near Wardha it stopped for a long time, and she noticed she had pressed the pen so hard it had gone right through the page.

qa.q: What was in Irawati's notebook?
qa.a: A diagram, with arrows in two colours.

qa.q: Why does "It makes total sense" feel like enough of an answer to Irawati?
qa.a: Understanding the breakup as a textbook cycle gives her control and keeps the hurt at a distance; the analysis is real, but it lets her skip how she actually feels 😔

qa.q: What could Irawati do once the call drops and she is alone with the notebook?
qa.a: She could take the pen pushed through the page as a sign of feeling and let herself name it, perhaps writing how it hurt instead of adding to the diagram.

qa.q: What is it like for Mitali to get a theory in reply to "how are you?"
qa.a: Mitali may feel shut out and worried, since the careful explanation answers a different question and leaves Mitali unsure how to help.

grounding: Illustrates a student on a stuffy, badly connected train explaining a breakup through attachment styles and a diagram while avoiding the hurt, until the feeling leaks out through the pen.
